extracted.intended_audience: bankruptcy lawyers, judges, and legal scholars (mass-tort and Chapter 11 practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and interpretive criteria for assessing whether a Chapter 11 plan may extinguish claims against nondebtors (nonconsensual third‑party releases), including textual, contextual, historical, and policy considerations in bankruptcy law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative claims resolution under §1123(b)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bankruptcy court may resolve derivative claims under §1123(b)(3) because those claims belong to the debtor’s estate (the named plaintiff is nominal; the substantive claim belongs to the corporation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples such as In re Ontos, Inc., and corporation law authorities explaining that derivative actions substantively belong to the corporation; apply §541(a) (claims belonging to the estate) when the claim is truly estate property. Do not conflate this power with authority to extinguish claims that belong to third‑party victims rather than to the debtor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of §1123(b) regarding nondebtor claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of §1123(b) are read as concerning the debtor’s rights and responsibilities and do not, without more, allow releases that extinguish claims victims and creditors hold against nondebtors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ejusdem generis canon and read the catchall in light of the five paragraphs that precede it; when preceding provisions relate to the debtor, the catchall should not be read to authorize extinguishing third‑party claims without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of statutory text over policy-driven readings
rubrics_metrics.description: While bankruptcy law may serve collective‑action purposes, courts must not treat such purposes as a roving commission to override clear statutory text; 'no statute pursues a single policy at all costs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resolving statutory meaning, prioritize the text and how far Congress has gone in pursuing a policy; consider that competing mechanisms (legislation, class actions, settlements) also address collective-action problems and the text must be decisive where clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency requirement for §1123(b)(6) provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any plan term adopted under §1123(b)(6) must not be 'inconsistent with the applicable provisions of' the Bankruptcy Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to Chapter 11 as a whole; if a proposed §1123(b)(6) term would conflict with other code provisions (e.g., rules limiting discharge or who may receive a discharge), that interpretation is implausible. Use Chapter 11 context to test proposed readings of §1123(b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge reserved to the debtor
rubrics_metrics.description: The code generally reserves the benefit of a discharge to 'the debtor'—the entity that files for bankruptcy—so a plan that effectively affords a nondebtor a discharge usually reserved for the debtor is inconsistent with code rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on §1141(d)(1)(A), §524(e), §§727(a)–(b) to evaluate whether a plan improperly seeks to give nondebtors debtor-like discharge relief; treat attempts to confer such relief skeptically absent explicit congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on scope of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Discharge has statutory limits: debtors must come forward with virtually all assets; discharge does not reach claims based on fraud or alleging willful and malicious injury; it cannot affect jury trial rights for personal injury or wrongful death claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply §§541(a)(1), 548; §§523(a)(2), (4), (6); and 28 U.S.C. §1411(a) when assessing whether proposed plan relief exceeds ordinary discharge scope. If nondebtors seek to extinguish claims (e.g., wrongful death, fraud) without committing equivalent assets, that suggests an impermissible overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asbestos exception indicates narrow congressional authorization for third‑party injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has authorized courts to enjoin claims against third parties without their consent in a single, specific context—certain asbestos-related bankruptcies under §524(g); that narrow, explicit authorization makes it unlikely §1123(b)(6) should be read to provide similar broad authority generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat §524(g) as an example of how Congress would express novel, extraordinary power; absence of comparable explicit text for other contexts weighs against reading §1123(b)(6) as authorizing nonconsensual third‑party releases broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot circumvent discharge limits by labeling relief a 'release'
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling the relief sought as a 'release' rather than a 'discharge' does not avoid the underlying statutory limits; substantive effect controls over terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the practical effect of the proposed relief—if it extinguishes victims’ claims without consent and confers debtor-like protection on nondebtors, the code’s limitations remain implicated regardless of labels; releases are traditionally consensual settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practice informs interpretation re: discharge to nondebtors
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-code practice (1800–1978) generally reserved discharge benefits to the debtor who offered a 'fair and full surrender' of property; no historic practice suggests courts could discharge claims by nondebtors against other nondebtors without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical statutes and cases (e.g., Sturges v. Crowninshield, Bankruptcy Acts) to interpret ambiguous provisions; absence of historical precedent for nondebtor discharges counsels against broad modern readings absent clear congressional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy arguments cannot override statutory limits—role of Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Even persuasive policy reasons (e.g., facilitating a settlement that enlarges the estate) do not permit courts to read statutes as authorizing relief they do not in fact authorize; Congress is the proper actor to make such policy judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties press policy consequences of a narrow textual reading (e.g., that victims would receive less without a nonconsensual release), acknowledge the policy point but defer to Congress to change the statutory framework if it chooses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensual third‑party release distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Consensual third‑party releases offered in connection with a bankruptcy plan pose different questions and remain distinct from the nonconsensual releases at issue; consensual releases may rest on different legal grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret a ruling on nonconsensual releases as invalidating consensual releases or plans that provide for full satisfaction of third‑party claims; evaluate consensual releases on their own statutory and equitable footing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑debtor releases as a bankruptcy tool (dissenting view)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the view expressed by the dissent, §1123(b)(6)'s term 'appropriate' and longstanding bankruptcy practice support the idea that nondebtor releases can be appropriate and essential in mass‑tort bankruptcies to build the estate and provide substantial, equitable recoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach, courts consider whether the release is necessary to facilitate a fair settlement, enlarges the estate materially (bringing nondebtor assets into the pool), and achieves equitable distribution for victims; treat historical practice and precedent approving nondebtor releases as supporting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Releases when indemnification creates de facto debtor suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Where officers or directors are indemnified by the debtor, a suit against those indemnified nondebtors may be 'in essence a suit against the debtor' and could deplete the estate, justifying treatment similar to direct claims against the debtor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess indemnification arrangements and the realistic source of recovery—if judgments against nondebtors would be paid from debtor assets, that practical effect bears on whether bankruptcy relief affecting such claims can be justified to solve collective‑action problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation thresholds and binding effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan may be confirmed even without unanimity if creditors holding more than one‑half in number and at least two‑thirds in amount of claims in every class accept the plan (§§1126(c), 1129(a)(8)(A)); once confirmed, creditors are bound by the plan's distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Chapter 11 voting and confirmation framework to evaluate whether a plan is 'consensual' for confirmation purposes and to understand how collective resolution mechanisms can bind dissenting creditors and solve holdout problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy as a collective‑action mechanism in mass‑tort cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Bankruptcy is designed to solve the collective‑action problem by pausing litigation, consolidating claims, and enabling fair, equitable distribution of estate assets among current and future victims—often reducing administrative costs compared to alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing proposed plan provisions in mass‑tort bankruptcies, consider the collective‑action rationale: whether bankruptcy (and any related releases or settlements) meaningfully coordinates claimants, prevents a race to the courthouse, and increases the pool of recoverable funds for victims and creditors.
